slides.title: Chapter 11: The Blockchain
slides.sub: How a block is built, how blocks are linked, how a merkle tree vouches for them, and which chain to test on

items.body: Picture: the Bitcoin logo, public domain (Wikimedia Commons). Python 3.14.6; Bitcoin Core 31.1 results are one recorded run, read back here.

slides.notes: This deck explains what a block is, how blocks are chained and named, how a merkle tree summarises transactions, and how Bitcoin's test chains differ. Every number on a result picture was computed with the chapter's own Python library or read from one recorded run of Bitcoin Core 31.1.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.sub: Three parts; every number is a slide you can jump to

items.label: code examples with a picture of each result

slides.notes: The route has three parts that follow the order of the chapter. Four true stories and seventeen code examples are spread across them. The examples are listed in the same order in the chapter code tab of the course page, so every listing here can be run and edited there.
slides.take: Three parts, seventeen examples, four true stories

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.sub: Each has an answer on a slide; we return to them in the summary

items: Which six fields make the 80-byte header of a block?
How is a block named, and where in the chain is it?
Why does changing one old block break every later one?
How can one root hash stand for thousands of transactions?
How short is the proof that one transaction is in a block?
How do testnet, signet and regtest differ, and when do I use each?
Why did testnet4 replace testnet3?

slides.notes: The seven questions are the chapter's own, rewritten so that each has an answer on a slide. We return to them in the summary. A reader who can answer all seven has understood the chapter.

slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Structure of a Block
items.meaning: An 80-byte header, a count of transactions, then the transactions themselves.
items.analogy: Think of a parcel with a label on top, an item count, then the items.

items.label: Block Header
items.meaning: Six fixed fields in 80 bytes that summarise the whole block.
items.analogy: Think of the cover page of a report that lists what follows.

items.label: Block Identifiers: Block Header Hash and Block Height

items.analogy: Think of a person's fingerprint and their seat number in a queue.

items.label: The Genesis Block
items.meaning: Block zero, mined on 3 January 2009, has no parent and quotes a newspaper headline.
items.analogy: Think of the first page of a diary, with no page before it.

slides.title: A block is header, count, transactions
slides.sub: Sizes of the genesis block, rebuilt from the source code

groups.note: The genesis block's only transaction is rebuilt from the constants in the source code.
A block is an 80-byte header, a count of transactions, then the transactions.
Bitcoin Core's own genesis block on a private chain has the same size.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library of the page, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: bytes of each part, 285 in all
Core's own genesis block on the private chain is also 285 bytes.

slides.notes: The genesis block is the smallest block there is. Its header takes 80 bytes, a count byte says there is one transaction, and the transaction fills the rest. Bitcoin Core on a private chain reports the same total. It is example 1 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Header, count byte and transaction make the whole block

slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Linking Blocks in the Blockchain
items.meaning: Each header holds the hash of its parent, so the blocks form one chain.
items.analogy: Think of train carriages, each coupled to the one before.

items.label: blockchain
items.meaning: The chain of blocks, each linked to its parent, that every node keeps.
items.analogy: Think of layers of a glacier: disturb one and every later layer is disturbed.

items.label: parent blocks
items.meaning: The block that a header names as the one before it.
items.analogy: Think of the parent named on a child's birth certificate.

items.label: genesis block
items.meaning: The only block with no parent; its hash is fixed in the software.
items.analogy: Think of the founder at the top of a family tree.

slides.notes: These cards cover Linking Blocks in the Blockchain, blockchain, parent blocks and genesis block. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 11.

slides.title: Six fields in 80 bytes
slides.sub: A header of the private chain, cut at fixed places

groups.note: The header of block 480 on the private chain is 80 bytes of hexadecimal.

rows: widths = [y - x for x, y in zip(cuts, cuts[1:])]
groups.note: Six fields follow one another; their widths are the gaps between the cut points.
The compact target, bits, is read back from the same bytes.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library of the page, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: bytes per field, 80 in all
The same bytes give the version 0x20000000 and the compact target 207fffff.

slides.notes: Version, previous block, merkle root, time, bits and nonce always sit in the same places. Four plus thirty-two plus thirty-two plus three times four make eighty. That fixed size is what makes headers cheap to store and check. It is example 2 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Every header has the same six fields in the same order and widths

slides.title: The block and the chain: concepts (3 of 5)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: child blocks
items.meaning: Blocks that name an earlier block as parent; one parent may have several children.
items.analogy: Think of two children of one parent, only one of whom carries the family on.

items.label: blocks
items.meaning: Bundles of transactions with a header, added to the chain about every ten minutes.
items.analogy: Think of pages of a ledger, sealed when full.

items.label: block header hash
items.meaning: The double SHA-256 of the 80 header bytes: the name of the block.
items.analogy: Think of a fingerprint taken from the block and never printed inside it.

slides.notes: These cards cover child blocks, blocks and block header hash. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 11.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Time, target and difficulty
slides.sub: Three numbers that the header carries

groups.note: The first block's time is a count of seconds since 1 January 1970.
Median time past is the middle one of the last eleven timestamps.
Bits packs a target; difficulty says how much smaller it is than the easiest.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library of the page, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: time, target and difficulty
The easiest target has 224 bits; the difficulty is how many times smaller a target is.

slides.notes: The time field counts seconds since 1970. Median time past takes the middle of eleven timestamps, so a single lying clock cannot move it. Bits packs the target, and difficulty compares it with the easiest target. It is example 3 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Bits is a compressed target; a smaller target means more difficulty

items.label: block height
items.meaning: The number of blocks between a block and the genesis block.
items.analogy: Think of the floors of a building counted from the ground.

items.label: Bitcoin Core
items.meaning: The reference software that checks every rule and stores the chain.
items.analogy: Think of the rulebook and the referee in one program.

items.label: Nakamoto, Satoshi
items.meaning: The pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin, who mined the genesis block and wrote the 2008 paper.
items.analogy: Think of an author known only by a pen name.

slides.notes: These cards cover block height, Bitcoin Core and Nakamoto, Satoshi. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 11.

slides.title: The first block quotes a newspaper
slides.sub: Message, time and name of block zero

groups.note: The text that the creator wrote into the first block is saved in the source code.
A block's name starts with zeros: count them in the genesis block's hash.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library of the page, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: block zero
The message reads: The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks.

slides.notes: The creator wrote a newspaper headline into the first block. The block hash, found by trying nonces, starts with ten zero digits. That is the work that made the block expensive to forge. It is example 4 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The ten zeros at the start of the name are the proof of work

slides.title: The Times in the first block
slides.sub: A newspaper headline nailed into the first block

items.cap: Bust of Satoshi Nakamoto, Budapest - Fekist, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHAT: Satoshi Nakamoto wrote the headline of The Times of 3 January 2009 into the first block: Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks.
WHY: The text proves the block is not older than that day, and the book adds that it recalls why an independent monetary system matters.
HOW: The chapter rebuilt the block from the constants in chainparams.cpp and hashed it to 000000000019d668; its 50 coins can never be spent.
SO WHAT: A date quoted inside a block proves the block is not older.

items.body: Stand-in picture: a statue, not the creator (unknown)

items.who: Satoshi Nakamoto, the pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin, and Alistair Darling, then Chancellor of the Exchequer of the United Kingdom
items.where: the first block of the Bitcoin chain, quoting The Times of London

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2009-01-03. The genesis block of Bitcoin has the timestamp 1231006505, which is 18:15:05 UTC on 3 January 2009. The lesson is that a date quoted inside a block proves the block is not older.

slides.title: The block and the chain: concepts (5 of 5)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: linking blocks in blockchain
items.meaning: Each block commits to its parent's hash, so rewriting history means redoing all later work.
items.analogy: Think of a wax seal pressed over the seal of the previous letter.

items.label: BIP 34
items.meaning: The proposal that puts the block height at the start of every coinbase script.
items.analogy: Think of a page number written on the first line of each page.

items.label: Bitcoin network
items.meaning: The peer-to-peer system of nodes that relay blocks and transactions.
items.analogy: Think of a postal system where every office copies the letters it sees.

slides.notes: These cards cover linking blocks in blockchain, BIP 34 and Bitcoin network. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 11.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Hash twice to get the name
slides.sub: A block is named by the double SHA-256 of its header

groups.note: A block is named by hashing its 80-byte header twice with SHA-256.
Hash once, then hash twice; only the second is the name Core uses.
The name is stored nowhere inside the block; every node recomputes it.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library of the page, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: one hash and two
Only the double hash starts with zeros and matches the name in the source.

slides.notes: One SHA-256 gives a different value from the block's name. Only the second hash, taken over the first, equals the hash in the source code. Every node recomputes it, so no one has to trust a stored name. It is example 5 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The name is computed again by every node; it is never stored in the block

slides.title: Height in the coinbase script
slides.sub: BIP 34 and the hundred-block wait

groups.note: Since BIP 34 the first bytes of the coinbase script carry the block's height.

rows: heights = sorted(L.bip34_height(v) for v in c.values())
groups.note: Read the height back from the script of each recorded block.
A coinbase may be spent only with 100 confirmations: 99 failed, 100 passed.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library of the page, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: heights decoded from eight coinbase scripts
Spending after 99 confirmations: refused. After 100: allowed.

slides.notes: Since BIP 34 the first bytes of the coinbase script spell the block height. We decode eight recorded scripts and get the heights back. Core refused to spend a reward after 99 confirmations and accepted it after 100. It is example 6 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A newly mined reward cannot be spent until 100 blocks are on top of it

slides.title: Changing one block breaks the chain
slides.sub: Ten headers, one bit flipped

groups.note: Ten consecutive headers of the private chain, each taken apart.

rows: link = lambda x, y: y['prev'] == x['hash']
groups.note: Each header names its parent: count the links that hold.
Flip one bit in header 3: which links break, and how many headers must be mined again?

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library of the page, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: one bit flipped in header 3
The change cannot stay hidden: header 4 no longer names its parent.

slides.notes: Each header holds the hash of its parent. Flip a single bit in header 3 and the link of header 4 no longer fits. To make the chain valid again, seven headers must be mined once more. It is example 7 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Alter block 3 and you must mine seven headers again

slides.title: A fork, and the odds of catching up
slides.sub: Two children of one parent, and Nakamoto's formula

groups.note: Two children of one parent block, both at height 511: a fork.
One more block on one child decides which branch is the active chain.
Nakamoto's odds that a ten percent attacker ever catches up, z blocks behind.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library of the page, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: chance of catching up, attacker with 10 percent
Both children had one parent: yes. The longer branch became active: yes.

slides.notes: Two blocks were mined on the same parent at height 511. One more block on the first child made it the active chain. The formula from the white paper shows how fast an attacker with ten percent falls behind. It is example 8 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A fork ends when one branch grows longer; an attacker's odds fall fast

slides.title: Merkle trees
slides.sub: A merkle tree is a knockout draw that ends with one winner, the root.

items.meaning: Pairs of hashes are hashed again until one root remains in the header.
items.analogy: Think of a knockout draw with one winner at the top.

items.meaning: A path of sibling hashes proves one transaction without the whole block.
items.analogy: Think of subtotals that prove one line of a ledger.

items.meaning: Repeating the last hash can make two lists share one root.
items.analogy: Think of a lone dancer paired with their own mirror image.

slides.notes: A merkle tree squeezes thousands of transactions into one hash in the header. We build a small tree, follow a proof of a few hashes, and meet the weakness that comes from repeating the last hash.

slides.title: Merkle trees: key concepts (1 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Merkle Trees
items.meaning: A tree of hashes: each parent hashes its two children and the top is a single root.
items.analogy: Think of a knockout tournament, matched in pairs until one name is left.

items.label: Merkle Trees and Lightweight Clients
items.meaning: A light client keeps headers only and asks for a short proof that a transaction is in a block.
items.analogy: Think of checking one ledger line against a signed total using subtotals.

items.label: binary hash trees
items.meaning: Every node has two children, so a tree over many leaves is only a few levels deep.
items.analogy: Think of a sports bracket folded in pairs.

items.label: balanced merkle trees
items.meaning: An odd level is padded by repeating its last hash, so every level pairs up.
items.analogy: Think of a lone dancer given a mirror image as partner.

slides.notes: These cards cover Merkle Trees, Merkle Trees and Lightweight Clients, binary hash trees and balanced merkle trees. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 11.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Pair, hash, repeat
slides.sub: A merkle tree of four, and of three, transactions

groups.note: Four transaction ids of a private block become the tree's bottom level.
Hash the pairs level by level; the top must equal the root in the header.
With three leaves the last one is paired with itself.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library of the page, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: hashes per level, 4 and 3 transactions
The rebuilt root equals the one in the header: yes. Three leaves still make three levels.

slides.notes: Four transaction ids make two hashes, then one root. The root equals the value in the block header. With three ids the last one is repeated, which gives the same number of levels. It is example 9 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: An odd level is completed by pairing the last hash with itself

slides.title: Merkle trees: key concepts (2 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: authentication path
items.meaning: The sibling hashes from a leaf up to the root; with them anyone can recompute the root.
items.analogy: Think of the receipts that prove one subtotal belongs in the grand total.

items.label: merkle path
items.meaning: Another name for the authentication path: one sibling hash for each level.
items.analogy: Think of directions that list each turn on the way up a staircase.

items.label: lightweight clients
items.meaning: Wallets that download headers only and verify transactions with merkle proofs.
items.analogy: Think of a reader who keeps the table of contents, not the whole book.

slides.notes: These cards cover authentication path, merkle path and lightweight clients. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 11.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: A proof of four hashes
slides.sub: One transaction of sixteen, proved with its siblings

groups.note: Block 16 holds sixteen transactions; prove that the eleventh is among them.
The path is four sibling hashes of 32 bytes; following it rebuilds the root.
A proof grows only with the logarithm of the number of transactions.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library of the page, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: proof bytes by number of transactions
A path of 4 hashes, 128 bytes, proves one of 16 transactions; it rebuilds the root: yes.

slides.notes: To prove one transaction we hand over the sibling hash at each level. Following them upward rebuilds the root in the header. Doubling the block adds a single hash to the proof. It is example 10 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The proof grows slowly: 16,000 transactions need 14 hashes

slides.title: Ralph Merkle's hash tree
slides.sub: One small hash that vouches for a whole list

items.cap: Ralph Merkle - david.orban (Flickr), CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHAT: Ralph Merkle patented the hash tree in 1979; United States patent 4,309,569 was published on 5 January 1982, with Stanford University as assignee.
WHY: A tree of hashes lets one small root vouch for a long list, which is how a block header covers every transaction.
HOW: The 40 transaction ids of block 277,315 were hashed in pairs, six levels up, to the root in its header.
SO WHAT: A small summary can vouch for a large list.

items.who: Ralph Merkle, the cryptographer who patented the hash tree, and Stanford University, the assignee of the patent
items.where: Stanford University in California; United States patent 4309569, published on 5 January 1982

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 1982-01-05. Ralph Merkle patented the hash tree in 1979, and the United States patent 4309569, Method of providing digital signatures, was published on 5 January 1982 with the Board of Trustees of Stanford University as assignee. The lesson is that a small summary can vouch for a large list.

slides.title: Two lists, one root
slides.sub: A weakness of the tree and Core's answer

groups.note: Repeating the last two ids of six transactions gives the same merkle root.
Two different lists, one root: the first weakness.
Core received such a mutated block and refused it; the original stayed.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library of the page, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: the duplicate weakness
Same header, different lists: Core must refuse the copy by its content.

slides.notes: Repeating the last two ids of six transactions gives the same root as the plain list. A block with such a copy therefore looks valid by its header. Core received one in a test and rejected it as a duplicate. It is example 11 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Core refuses a block whose transaction list repeats a hash

slides.title: A light client needs 248 bytes
slides.sub: A merkleblock proof read apart

groups.note: A light client asks a full node for a proof: a header plus a few hashes.
Only the header, a count and a handful of hashes cross the wire.
The proof says one transaction of sixteen is in the block, in under 250 bytes.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library of the page, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: the merkleblock proof
Five hashes and a header stand in for sixteen transactions.

slides.notes: A light client asks a full node for a proof. It gets the header, the number of transactions, five hashes and some flags. Core confirmed that the proof contains exactly the transaction we asked about. It is example 12 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A phone can check one payment without the other fifteen transactions

slides.title: Test blockchains
slides.sub: A test chain is a rehearsal room: same stage, no real audience.

items.meaning: Mainnet and four test chains share one code base with different constants.
items.analogy: Think of five stages built to one plan with different props.

items.meaning: A public test chain with worthless coins and a minimum-difficulty rule.
items.analogy: Think of a sandpit in a park where castles may be knocked down.

items.meaning: Signet needs a signature for each block; regtest is private and mined on demand.
items.analogy: Think of a club with a doorman, and a private rehearsal room.

slides.notes: Bitcoin has more than one chain. Testnet, signet and regtest follow the same rules with different constants, so developers can experiment without real money. We compare them and read their constants.

slides.title: Test blockchains: key concepts (1 of 5)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Bitcoin's Test Blockchains
items.meaning: Separate chains with Bitcoin's rules and worthless coins, for experiments.
items.analogy: Think of a flight simulator, a training pitch and the match: same rules, different stakes.

items.label: Testnet: Bitcoin's Testing Playground
items.meaning: A public test chain whose coins have no value.
items.analogy: Think of a sandpit in a park, where castles may be knocked down.

items.label: Using testnet
items.meaning: Point a wallet or node at testnet and take free coins from a faucet.
items.analogy: Think of practising with play money.

items.label: Problems with testnet
items.meaning: Its minimum-difficulty rule let miners flood it with blocks, so testnet4 replaced it.
items.analogy: Think of a sandpit that nobody tidies.

slides.notes: These cards cover Bitcoin's Test Blockchains, Testnet: Bitcoin's Testing Playground, Using testnet and Problems with testnet. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 11.

slides.sub: Ports and expected sizes from the source file

slides.title: When the sandbox was flooded
slides.sub: A test network without incentives gets flooded

items.cap: Children in a sandpit - Shixart1985, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHAT: On 4 May 2024 Jameson Lopp described how the minimum-difficulty rule of testnet3 let miners create hundreds of blocks in a single day.
WHY: A test network without incentives needs rules against vandals, so testnet4 and BIP 94, written by Fabian Jahr, replaced it.
HOW: BIP 94 notes that three years of blocks were mined in a few weeks; on 15 October 2026 testnet3 stood at height 5,189,394, testnet4 at 156,618.
SO WHAT: Core 31.1 still starts testnet3 but its help says that the support will be removed.

items.body: Stand-in picture: a sandpit stands for the test network

items.who: Jameson Lopp, who wrote the blog post, and Fabian Jahr, who wrote BIP 94 for testnet4
items.where: the blog of Jameson Lopp, the bitcoin/bips repository, and Bitcoin Core 28.0

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2024-05-04. On 4 May 2024 Jameson Lopp published Griefing Bitcoin's Testnet, which describes how the testnet3 rule of minimum difficulty after 20 minutes lets miners create hundreds of blocks in a single day. The lesson is that a test network without incentives needs rules against vandals.

slides.title: A test network with a doorman
slides.sub: Replace mining by a signature and the test network stays calm

items.cap: Signet ring of Ramesses II - akhenatenator, CC0 1.0, Flickr

items: WHAT: BIP 325 defines signet: a block is valid only if it carries a solution to a challenge script, so its creators decide who may make blocks.
WHY: Replace mining by a signature and a test network stays calm, with no flood of blocks.
HOW: The default challenge is a 1-of-2 multisig, and its four magic bytes, 0a03cf40, start the double SHA-256 of that script.
SO WHAT: Core 0.21.0 added it; on 15 October 2026 the tip was at height 326,440, 2.27 times the book's listing.

slides.title: The chapter in five lines
slides.sub: One line per idea, each provable from its slides

items: A block is an 80-byte header of six fields plus its transactions; its name is the double hash of the header.
Each header names its parent, so changing one old block breaks every later link; a fork ends when one branch is longer.
A merkle tree puts all transactions under one root, and a path of a few hashes proves one of them.
The tree has a known weakness: repeating the last hash can give two lists one root, and Core refuses the copy.
Testnet, signet and regtest share the rules with other constants; each serves another stage of development.

slides.notes: These five lines are the deck in miniature. A line that feels unproven should send you back to its code slide, because every figure in it was computed there. The chapter code tab of the course page reruns all seventeen examples.
